lesson.title: Filling In the Gaps: Continuous Variables
lesson.summary: This section defines continuous variables as quantitative variables that can take any value within a range, contrasts them with discrete variables, and revisits the classroom height data to illustrate the idea of measurement precision.
lesson.body:
A continuous variable is a quantitative variable whose possible values can fall anywhere within a range, with no gaps between one possible value and the next. Where the previous section described discrete variables as isolated points on a number line, a continuous variable fills in the entire line, or at least the realistic stretch of it, without any breaks. The clearest sign that a variable is continuous is that it comes from measuring rather than counting. Height, weight, time, temperature, and distance are all continuous, because between any two possible values, no matter how close together, another value is always theoretically possible.

Height, from the classroom dataset introduced earlier, is a continuous variable. The 8 recorded heights were 61, 64, 58, 66, 63, 59, 65, and 60 inches. But those exact whole numbers are really just rounded measurements. A student's true height might actually be 60.7 inches, recorded as 61 because the tape measure the teacher used was only precise to the nearest inch. With a more precise instrument, that same student could be measured as 60.68 inches, or 60.683 inches, and so on. In principle there is no smallest gap between possible heights, only a limit set by how precisely our measuring tools can measure. This is the key difference from a discrete variable like number of siblings, where 1 and 2 are the only options and nothing can ever fall between them.

This idea of measurement precision leads to a useful worked example. Consider the average height already computed for the classroom dataset: adding 61, 64, 58, 66, 63, 59, 65, and 60 gives a total of 496 inches, and dividing by the 8 students gives an average of 496 divided by 8, which equals exactly 62.0 inches. Because height is continuous, this average of 62.0 inches is a perfectly sensible, physically meaningful number, representing a genuinely possible height that some student really could have. Compare this to the earlier discrete example, number of siblings, where the average of 1.25 could not correspond to any real student. Continuous variables allow their summary statistics to land anywhere along the range and still represent a physically realizable value, precisely because the underlying scale has no gaps to avoid.

Because continuous variables can take on infinitely many possible values within any range, they are typically displayed using histograms, which group nearby values into intervals called bins, rather than bar graphs or dot plots, which work best when there are only a small number of distinct, separated values to display. Recognizing whether a quantitative variable is discrete or continuous, using the counting versus measuring test introduced across these last two sections, is one of the first decisions to make whenever you sit down to graph or summarize a new dataset.
